articles.title: Serval: felino africano é achado em quintal durante incêndio nos EUA | G1
articles.standfirst: Serval era criado de forma ilegal em um cercado de quintal em Marrero, na Louisiana; animal foi retirado do local e ficará sob cuidados temporários até ser levado para um ambiente adequado.
articles.summary: O serval africano foi resgatado de um cercado ilegal em Marrero após ser descoberto por bombeiros e aguarda transferência para um ambiente adequado.
articles.body:
Serval encontrado em casa dos EUA. — Foto: John McCusker/JPaws/Reprodução/Facebook

Bombeiros foram chamados para apagar um incêndio em uma casa em Marrero, na Louisiana, nos Estados Unidos, na terça-feira (15), e acabaram encontrando um serval, felino selvagem de médio porte nativo da África Subsaariana, em um cercado no quintal da residência .

Uma instituição local de resgate de animais, a JPAWS, foi chamada para retirar o animal do local. O serval foi contido e colocado em uma gaiola.

A JPAWS levou o serval para suas instalações e chegou a avaliar a possibilidade de mantê-lo temporariamente no zoológico Audubon, em Nova Orleans. No entanto, um porta-voz da instituição afirmou que o zoológico não planejava receber o animal.

Assim, o animal retirado da casa em Marrero será mantido temporariamente sob os cuidados da JPAWS até que seja encontrado um local permanente e adequado para ele.

Em uma publicação no Facebook, a instituição informou que o serval nasceu em cativeiro. A posse legal de um animal desse tipo exige uma licença para animais exóticos.

A agência afirmou, também, que servais não são bons animais de estimação. Eles marcam território, não podem ser completamente treinados para viver dentro de casa e podem destruir móveis. Segundo a JPAWS, eles normalmente se tornam agressivos quando atingem a maturidade.

Os servais também têm instinto de caça e comportamento territorial e precisam de espaço e estímulos. Em cativeiro, segundo a agência, podem sofrer estresse crônico por não conseguirem realizar comportamentos naturais e saudáveis.

Servais são conhecidos pela capacidade de saltar cerca de 2 metros de altura e têm características que podem fazê-los parecer semelhantes a gatos domésticos. Apesar disso, especialistas e organizações de proteção animal destacam que eles necessitam de cuidados, alimentação e espaço diferentes dos exigidos por gatos domésticos.

Serval encontrado em casa nos EUA e resgatado pela Jefferson Parish Animal Welfare Service-in de New Orleans. — Foto: John McCusker/JPAWS/Reprodução/Facebook

articles.title: O que está por trás do acordo entre EUA, Dinamarca e Groenlândia | G1
articles.standfirst: Donald Trump afirmou que tratado será 'para sempre'. Ilha guarda recursos naturais importantes e está localizada em área estratégica para EUA, Europa e China.
articles.summary: Donald Trump afirmou que tratado será 'para sempre'. Ilha guarda recursos naturais importantes e está localizada em área estratégica para EUA, Europa e China.
articles.body:
O presidente dos Estados Unidos , Donald Trump , anunciou nesta sexta-feira (18) que os norte-americanos serão responsáveis pelo controle da segurança da Groenlândia "para sempre". Um acordo sobre o tema deve ser assinado com a Dinamarca na próxima semana.

O tratado representa uma conquista importante para Trump, que há muito tempo defende a anexação da ilha pelos EUA. Nos últimos meses, ele fez diversas declarações sobre o território — que pertence à Dinamarca, mas tem governo autônomo e discute a possibilidade de independência.

Segundo o presidente norte-americano, a Groenlândia tem um papel estratégico para a segurança dos EUA e de outros países.

"Precisamos da Groenlândia para a segurança internacional. Precisamos dela", afirmou em uma entrevista em dezembro de 2025. "Odeio colocar dessa forma, mas temos que ficar com ela."

Trump também chegou a dizer que poderia usar a força para conquistar a Groenlândia e ameaçou aplicar tarifas contra a União Europeia caso o território não fosse cedido aos EUA. À época, autoridades da ilha e da Dinamarca afirmavam que o território não estava à venda.

O tom mudou no início deste ano, quando começaram as conversas entre Dinamarca, Groenlândia e Estados Unidos. A negociação foi baseada em um tratado de segurança no Ártico.

A primeira-ministra da Dinamarca, Mette Frederiksen, a presidente da Comissão Europeia, Ursula von der Leyen, e o primeiro-ministro da Groenlândia, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, visitam Qoornoq em 6 de setembro de 2026 — Foto: Mads Claus Rasmussen/REUTERS

Coberta em 80% por gelo e com 57 mil habitantes, a Groenlândia é a maior ilha do mundo e possui hidrocarbonetos e minerais importantes para a transição energética.

O território está geograficamente localizado na América do Norte, mas mantém fortes relações com a Dinamarca. A ilha, que já foi uma colônia dinamarquesa, passou a fazer parte do Reino da Dinamarca em 1953 e, até hoje, segue a Constituição dinamarquesa.

Em 2009, a Dinamarca autorizou a Groenlândia a ter um governo próprio e autônomo, permitindo até mesmo uma declaração de independência por meio de referendo.

Trump não foi o primeiro presidente dos Estados Unidos a tentar adquirir a ilha. Após o fim da Segunda Guerra Mundial, Harry Truman tentou comprá-la, oferecendo US$ 100 milhões em ouro. O objetivo era garantir um território estratégico para enfrentar as ameaças da Guerra Fria.

A proposta de Truman foi rejeitada, mas, no início da década de 1950, os Estados Unidos conseguiram instalar uma base militar na ilha com a autorização da Dinamarca.

Durante seu primeiro mandato como presidente, Trump afirmou que faria uma oferta para comprar a Groenlândia. Na época, as autoridades da ilha responderam que o território não estava à venda.

Em janeiro de 2025, Trump voltou a investir contra a Groenlândia. Ele argumenta que a ilha poderia servir como uma plataforma estratégica para monitorar ameaças vindas da Rússia e da Europa. A presença de radares e bases militares fortaleceria o sistema de defesa americano.

Além disso, radares instalados na região ajudariam a identificar navios e submarinos, principalmente russos, monitorando as águas entre a Islândia, a Grã-Bretanha e a própria Groenlândia.

E essa posição estratégica não vem de hoje. Durante a Guerra Fria, russos e americanos mantiveram armas nucleares e submarinos no Ártico.

Além do fatos militar, a ilha também é rica em minerais, petróleo e gás natural. No entanto, a extração de minerais enfrenta forte oposição de povos indígenas e restrições burocráticas do governo. Já a exploração de petróleo e gás natural é proibida por questões ambientais.

Navio de guerra da Otan navega durante treinamento militar no Ártico em janeiro de 2025. — Foto: Divulgação/Otan

Outro fator que aumenta a importância estratégica da região é o aquecimento do Ártico. O derretimento do gelo tende a ampliar a importância de portos e pode abrir novas rotas de navegação, mudando a dinâmica do comércio internacional.

Nesse contexto entra a China, que também tem interesse no Ártico. Uma nova rota marítima pela região poderia reduzir a distância percorrida por navios chineses em comparação com rotas tradicionais, além de passar ao lado da Rússia, uma das principais parceiras de Pequim.

Embora esteja distante cerca de 2 mil quilômetros do Ártico, a China investe na construção de navios quebra-gelo. O país também é o maior produtor mundial de carros elétricos e turbinas eólicas, setores que dependem de minerais considerados estratégicos.

Os Estados Unidos querem evitar que os chineses avancem na região.

Donald Trump, presidente dos EUA, em foto de 13 de setembro de 2026 — Foto: AP/Julia Demaree Nikhinson

Em uma publicação na rede social Truth Social, Trump afirmou que o acordo garante aos norte-americanos a capacidade de "para sempre" fazer o que for necessário para proteger a Groenlândia e os próprios EUA.

Segundo o presidente, o acordo fechado determina que nenhum adversário dos EUA poderá manter uma base ou presença militar na Groenlândia, nem fazer investimentos considerados sensíveis no território, sem autorização do governo americano.

"Começaremos imediatamente o processo de desenvolvimento de uma grande presença militar na parte apropriada da Groenlândia, que possui muitas dessas áreas", afirmou.

Dinamarca e Groenlândia elogiaram o acordo. O governo dinamarquês afirmou que o tratado reconhece a soberania do território, ao mesmo tempo que amplia a segurança na região.

Segundo a primeira-ministra do país, Mette Frederiksen, o tratado vai fortalecer a segurança no Ártico e no Atlântico Norte.

"É um acordo que fortalece nossa segurança comum no Ártico e na região do Atlântico Norte e, portanto, também é bom para a Otan e para a Europa", afirmou.

"O acordo ao mesmo tempo reconhece a soberania e a integridade territorial do Reino e o direito do povo groenlandês à autodeterminação."

Já o primeiro-ministro da Groenlândia, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, disse que o acordo com os EUA respeita e reconhece os interesses da Groenlândia. Segundo ele, a iniciativa será benéfica a "todos".

As partes ainda não revelaram detalhes sobre o texto do acordo, e o documento deve ser assinado na próxima semana, durante a Assembleia Geral da ONU.

5. Groenlândia pode se tornar parte dos EUA?

Donald Trump Jr. chegou há poucos dias a Nuuk, na Groenlândia — Foto: Emil Stach/Ritzau Scanpix/via REUTERS

Em 2009, a Dinamarca autorizou a Groenlândia a formar um governo próprio e autônomo, abrindo a possibilidade de uma declaração de independência por meio de referendo.

Com isso, na teoria, os habitantes da Groenlândia poderiam votar pela independência da ilha e, posteriormente, decidir se querem uma associação com os Estados Unidos. Na prática, porém, especialistas consideram essa hipótese pouco provável.

Uma pesquisa feita no país, no fim do ano passado, indicou que apenas 6% da população apoia a incorporação aos Estados Unidos.

articles.title: Newspaper headlines: 'His words were monstrous' and 'Russia to ramp up war'
articles.summary: The fallout from Earl Spencer's book about Princess Diana leads most papers on Saturday.
articles.body:
The Daily Telegraph has spoken to intelligence officials who warn that Russia may be planning to intensify hybrid attacks on European allies of Ukraine. The paper says intelligence services have monitored a potential "stealth mobilisation" of Russian personnel and assets, which coincides with plans to remove US military capabilities from Europe.

An investigation by the i Paper has found that the army relaxed its security vetting procedures for at least two years after the pandemic, allowing in a far-right extremist who supports Russia. Thirteen thousand recruits are reported to have been allowed to sign up without full background checks, sparking fears of espionage and infiltration.

The Times reports that the chancellor is considering lowering the threshold for the so-called mansion tax from £2m to £1.5m. Two sources from within government have told the paper there is a "live discussion" about the change, because of the effect of the Iran war on the cost of government borrowing.

The 83-year-old billionaire founder of the gambling group Betfred Fred Done has told the Financial Times of his gloomy outlook for the country. He says that he "would not wish to be reborn" in the UK and predicts that "the High Street will be dead" by 2030. He says if the chancellor raises taxes on slot machines in the Budget, he will close almost 500 of the firm's shops.

The Daily Mirror hears from fuel experts who say the price of diesel is likely to reach an all-time high next week. One haulage firm boss whose annual bills have increased by £350,000 this year tells the paper "we've been trading for more than 50 years and the past few months have been among the worst we've experienced".

The Sun devotes part of its editorial to the forthcoming MPs' committee investigation into the UK's lamentable performances at recent Eurovisions . "Here's our verdict, without the need for a time-consuming Parliamentary investigation", the paper says, "pick better tunes."

images.caption: Many of Saturday's papers continue their coverage of the fallout from Earl Spencer's book about his sister Diana, Princess of Wales. In an interview with the BBC, Earl Spencer said he was telling the truth about the nature of a phone call he had after his sister's death with the then Prince Charles. In excerpts published by the Daily Mail, the earl claimed King Charles III told him "we'll forget her soon enough", but Buckingham Palace said in a statement that fraternal grief could "colour memory". The Mail says Earl Spencer hit back at the King in a "defiant" interview.

articles.title: Extremely speedy action by probe agency can create doubt: SC
articles.summary: India News: New Delhi: The speed at which CBI sprang into action on a bribery complaint and laid a trap within hours to catch a public servant could give rise to .
articles.body: New Delhi: The speed at which CBI sprang into action on a bribery complaint and laid a trap within hours to catch a public servant could give rise to suspicion, which, Supreme Court said, could not be brushed aside and had to be examined.Finding fault with CBI's investigation, Justices Dipankar Datta and N K Singh acquitted the official in a two-decade-old case as he was not caught with the bribe money. It was an intermediary who accepted it and CBI failed to prove it was meant for the accused, SC said.The complaint made in 2005 alleged that the accused, working as a divisional security commissioner in Railway Protection Force, had demanded illegal gratification from subordinate officials for transfers and postings. CBI immediately lodged an FIR and laid a trap just hours later, catching the intermediary.The intermediary, who alleged that he accepted the bribe on behalf of the official, was given a pardon.SC said since the FIR was lodged on Aug 4, 2005, at 2pm and CBI decided to lay the trap on the same day, the agency must have verified the authenticity of the complaint before the trap was planned. "It is surprising that CBI started the investigation of a cognisable offence by way of verifying the complaint of bribery even before the formal FIR was lodged... The entire trap was arranged between 2 pm to 4.30pm. While the investigating agency cannot be faulted for organising the trap in such an extraordinarily speedy manner, it can raise certain doubts. The trial court, however, brushed aside the doubts raised by the appellant," the bench said.The court said criminality under Prevention of Corruption Act did not arise merely because money changed hands. "Before criminal liability can be fastened upon the public servant, the prosecution must establish by reliable evidence that the intermediary was acting under the authority, direction or for the benefit of the accused and that the demand itself was attributable to the accused. Mere receipt of money by a third person cannot automatically result in criminal liability being imputed to a public servant," it said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Mumbai man on knifing spree: Lane caked in blood, how  row over 'money' turned deadly for 15-year-old
articles.summary: MUMBAI: A  30-year-old man went on a knifing spree at Malwani on Friday morning, resulting in the death of a minor boy and leaving another person crit.
articles.body: MUMBAI: A 30-year-old man went on a knifing spree at Malwani on Friday morning, resulting in the death of a minor boy and leaving another person critical. The lane was caked in blood as police carted away a blood-soaked Rizwaan Qureshi, the accused, and took him into custody on murder charges.Police added that Qureshi was set to attack a third individual with the knife but locals caught him before he could do so and gave him a sound thrashing.The incident occurred around 10.30 am at New Collector’s Compound, Malwani. Qureshi had come to Mumbai 10 days ago and had been staying in Malwani. On Friday, he was asking for money and approached a shop in Gate no 6 area. A 15-year-old boy, Bunty Khan, was at the shop. Khan’s father runs his catering business from the shop, while the family lives on the first floor of the structure.Police said Qureshi asked Khan for some money and a glass of water. The teen responded that he could fetch water but would not give him any money. When the teen got some water, Qureshi slashed him on the neck with a knife. The teen suffered deep injuries and bled profusely.Qureshi then ventured further in the same lane and knifed a pedestrian, Chetan Patel, without any provocation. Patel was also slashed on the neck. Thereafter, Qureshi turned towards another house and was preparing to attack his third target. But before he could do so, bystanders summoned the courage to catch hold of him.They then proceeded to thrash him. The Malwani police were summoned and Qureshi was handed over to them.Khan and Patel were rushed to a govt hospital. However, Khan died due to the nature of injuries suffered. Patel was given treatment and is stable.A native of UP, Qureshi had lived in Malwani in the past before moving to Pune and later to Hyderabad. He used to do odd jobs, including selling sarees. Police are trying to establish the motive. They suspect Qureshi may have lost his cool after being denied money. Investigators will also verify if he is suffering from any mental health issues. articles.title: Trump’s Greenland deal: How Arctic pact bolsters Golden Dome against Russia, China
articles.summary: International News: US President Donald Trump announced on Friday that the Washington has reached an \"Infinite Life\" agreement with Denmark and Greenland giving America \".
articles.body: US President Donald Trump announced on Friday that the Washington has reached an "Infinite Life" agreement with Denmark and Greenland giving America "permanent control" over the island's security.He said the deal also bars any US adversary from keeping a military presence there. Trump called it an agreement with no end and said it would come at no cost to the United States."This is an “Infinite Life” Agreement, there is no end! We are very honored and proud of what has just taken place, and everything agreed to today will be cherished by the American People. We will immediately begin the process of developing a large Military presence in the appropriate part of Greenland, of which there are many," Trump wrote while annoucing the deal.What has actually been agreedDanish prime minister Mette Frederiksen said the deal does not hand the United States sovereignty over Greenland, describing it instead an arrangement that strengthens shared security in the Arctic and North Atlantic and recognises the Greenlandic people's right to self determination.The United States, Denmark and Greenland are expected to sign the text next week at the United Nations General Assembly in New York, reported CNBC. The official wording had not been released when Trump made his announcement. America already enjoys near total basing and overflight rights on the island under a treaty signed in 1951. Trump announces agreement with Denmark to secure ‘permanent’ control over Greenland’s security.Why Greenland matters for the Golden DomeGolden Dome is Trump’s proposed multi-layered missile defence system designed to detect, track and intercept ballistic, cruise and hypersonic missiles targeting the US. Greenland matters because of its location in the Arctic, particularly for monitoring missile activity from Russia and supporting early-warning capabilities.Greater US access to Greenland could therefore strengthen the Arctic component of Golden Dome, while limiting potential military or strategic access for China and Russia.The shortest route for a missile fired from Russia towards American cities runs over the North Pole, and Greenland sits almost exactly underneath that path. That geography is the whole reason the island matters to the Golden Dome project, because putting sensors, communications gear and interceptors closer to the pole gives defenders a better chance of destroying a missile early in its flight.The island is already doing part of this job. Pituffik Space Base, formerly known as Thule, lies above the Arctic Circle roughly halfway between Washington and Moscow, and its radar can watch deep into Russia and across the likely flight paths of Chinese missiles, buying American decision makers precious extra minutes.Trump wants Golden Dome fully working by January 2029 at a cost of 175 billion dollars, a timetable and price tag that seems doubtful. It has also been point out that interceptor tests over the past two decades have succeeded only about half the time, and under conditions far kinder than a real attack.Locking out Moscow and BeijingThe second purpose of the deal is to keep rivals out as Trump said no American adversary may ever build a base in Greenland, station forces there, or make sensitive investments, without express written approval from Washington.In plain terms, a Chinese state firm buying a stake in a Greenlandic mine or port would now need an American signature first. That single clause is aimed squarely at the quiet economic route into the Arctic that Beijing has used elsewhere.Moscow has already bristled at the idea, with Russian officials calling Golden Dome provocative and warned of military and technical countermeasures if American missile systems appear on the island.Greenland is also a mineral prize as official Danish and Greenlandic geological surveys estimate the island holds some 36 million tonnes of rare earth resources, alongside graphite, copper, nickel, zinc and tungsten, and it hosts deposits of 25 of the 34 raw materials the European Commission treats as critical. These metals go into electric motors, semiconductors and precision guided weapons.China currently produces roughly 60 per cent of the world's rare earths and controls about 85 per cent of processing capacity, which is why Western governments want another source. The Tanbreez project in southern Greenland, now 92.5 per cent owned by Nasdaq listed Critical Metals, is the furthest along, with full construction not expected before spring 2027.

articles.title: Watch: Iranian women run Tehran race event without hijab, defying compulsory rules
articles.summary: Middle East News: Videos of women taking part in a 10-kilometre road race in Tehran without wearing headscarves have gone viral, drawing attention in Iran where the hij.
articles.body: Videos of women taking part in a 10-kilometre road race in Tehran without wearing headscarves have gone viral, drawing attention in Iran where the hijab remains compulsory under law.Several women were seen running with their hair uncovered during Friday's Tehran 10K at Velayat Park. The organisers held separate races for men and women, with the women's event covering two laps of the 10-kilometre course.The race took place on the same day as the Janfadayan-e Iran rally, a large state-backed gathering elsewhere in Tehran attended by Revolutionary Guards, Basij members and volunteers pledging to defend the country.The two events were not connected. However, footage of the unveiled runners was also circulated by some state-affiliated accounts on X, drawing attention because public appearances without a hijab remain prohibited under Iranian law.Friday's scenes were particularly notable because authorities had previously taken action against organisers of a women's road race on Kish Island after participants were seen competing without headscarves.Hijab rules remain in forceIranian women have increasingly appeared in public without headscarves since the 2022 Woman, Life, Freedom protests, which erupted after the death of Mahsa "Jina" Amini while in morality police custody.Although uncovered hair has become increasingly common on Iranian streets and in some public spaces, compulsory hijab remains part of Iranian law. Enforcement continues in different forms, while government offices and many official establishments generally still require women to wear headscarves to enter.Parisa Arab, Iran's national record holder in the women's 5,000 metres, 10,000 metres and half marathon, won Friday's race.Arab later shared a video showing scenes from the event and her crossing the finish line. She said the encouragement from spectators gave her energy during the most difficult parts of the race.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: How Delhi executive Yuvraj Singh Manchanda's death unfolded: 'Body kept in car for 2 days, dumped, drowned, cremated'
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Police are probing whether the body of 31-year-old Yuvraj Singh Manchanda, an executive at Adani Realty, was kept inside a car for two days.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Police are probing whether the body of 31-year-old Yuvraj Singh Manchanda, an executive at Adani Realty, was kept inside a car for two days after he was allegedly murdered by two former colleagues.The accused couple, Anya Vats and her partner Sanyam Sachdeva, both residents of Gurgaon, have been arrested. Police said both have a criminal history.Investigators are also examining conflicting statements given by the couple about how long Yuvraj’s body remained inside their car and what happened before it was dumped in a drain.Conflicting accounts over body disposalPolice sources said Vats and Sachdeva initially told investigators that they kept Yuvraj’s body inside the vehicle for around seven hours. Their statements later changed, prompting investigators to verify the timeline.The couple have been taken to several locations as part of the investigation. Police are trying to establish where Yuvraj met them, how the alleged killing took place, where they travelled afterwards and the route they took before disposing of his body.According to the preliminary investigation, Vats and Sachdeva had asked Yuvraj to meet them near a mall in Sector 70, Gurgaon, on 6 September. Yuvraj reportedly reached the location in his own car, left it there and joined the couple in their vehicle.An argument allegedly broke out between them, following which Yuvraj was killed, police suspect.Investigators believe Vats and Sachdeva then parked the vehicle containing Yuvraj’s body and travelled to different locations using autos and cabs. They allegedly returned to the vehicle later and dumped the body in a drain near their home.The couple also told investigators that they drove around Gurgaon before parking the vehicle, looking for a place to dispose of the body.They later fled to Uttarakhand, where they were detained. Yuvraj’s decomposed body was found in the drain on 10 September.Police probe possible money disputeInvestigators are examining a possible monetary dispute between Yuvraj and the accused.Police said Vats and Sachdeva gave different accounts of the amount allegedly involved. They initially cited a dispute over Rs 5 lakh but later changed the figure to Rs 25 lakh.Police are verifying these claims and examining whether the dispute was connected to the trio’s professional dealings in the real estate sector.Yuvraj, Vats and Sachdeva had worked together at the same firm between 2019 and 2022. Yuvraj later moved to another job.Vats was allegedly removed from the company over financial irregularities, according to investigators. She and Sachdeva later worked as freelancers and became involved in property dealings.Police are investigating whether a dispute involving clients and real estate transactions contributed to the alleged confrontation.Accused couple's criminal recordsPolice said Vats has two cheating cases registered against her.One was registered at Parliament Street police station, where she is accused of allegedly cheating by posing as a government official. Another case was registered in Greater Noida.A domestic violence case was registered against Sachdeva by his wife, officers said.Investigators are examining these cases as part of their probe into the background of the accused.Autopsy says drowningThe autopsy report recorded drowning as the cause of Yuvraj’s death, police said.Investigators said there were no bullet injuries on his body, rejecting claims that he had been shot.Police also said the body appeared to have remained in water for several days.Investigators are awaiting further material, including Yuvraj’s belongings and the postmortem report from Gurgaon Police. They are also examining forensic evidence and the statements of the accused to establish the sequence of events.Family learns of death six days laterYuvraj’s family says they only learnt that his body had been found days after it was recovered.“Our mother is waiting for me to bring back something – anything to remember Yuvraj by. His clothes, his watch… or now, even his ashes,” said Karishma Manchanda, Yuvraj’s older sister.His body was found by Haryana Police on 10 September, but the family says they were informed only on 16 September.By then, his body had already been cremated by police.Karishma said her family has still not been given his remains. She said she learnt about the discovery of her brother’s body only after going to Badshahpur police station in Gurgaon on 16 September.The family was then told that Yuvraj’s body had been recovered six days earlier and had already been cremated.Police are now trying to establish the precise timeline of Yuvraj’s death, the period for which his body remained in the vehicle and the events that followed before it was dumped in the drain.(With inputs from Nikhil Sharma, G S Dhanush)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: Saudi Arabia issues first air raid alerts for Riyadh since Houthis escalated attacks
articles.summary: Residents later received the all-clear after explosions were reported in the capital.
articles.body:
Residents in Saudi Arabia's Riyadh have been given the all-clear after air raid alerts were issued and explosions were reported in the capital.

It was the first time alerts have been issued in Riyadh since the Houthis increased their attacks and declared a "maritime embargo" on the Saudis in July.

The Saudi Civil Defence sent alerts for the capital and several other regions late on Friday night and Saturday morning (local time) as the Kingdom's conflict with the Iran-backed Houthis continued to escalate.

Journalists from Reuters and AFP reported hearing explosions in the capital, but authorities have since said the danger has passed. Residents were urged to avoid gathering in crowds.

The Houthis recently seized control of the strategic port city of Mokha and Perim Island, a gateway to a key shipping route used by the Gulf state to export to Asia and Europe.

The Iran-backed group's military spokesman said the naval blockade was in retaliation for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in Houthi-controlled north-western Yemen.

Saudi vessels have relied on that stretch of the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz.

Last week, the Houthis attacked several Saudi oil facilities with drones and missiles, causing fires which led to operations being temporarily halted.

The attacks on Saudi oil assets have directly impacted global energy markets and the price of petrol and diesel in many countries has sharply risen in recent weeks, compounding already elevated costs caused by the blockades of the Strait of Hormuz.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the country's de facto ruler, has personally asked US President Donald Trump to take military action against the Houthis, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News, the BBC's US media partner.

Trump has so far declined to involve the US military directly, offering instead to assist with intelligence and targeting support, the sources said.

A senior Trump administration official told the BBC: "We are in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen government regarding regional stability."

Earlier this week, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea said the Houthis had launched drones and missiles at Saudi Arabia in retaliation for more than 450 Saudi air strikes on their territory over the past week.

The United Nations Security Council held an emergency meeting on Tuesday, during which both Yemen's government and Saudi Arabia called for more decisive action against the Houthis, who they accused of choking the Bab al-Mandab Strait as a way of applying economic pressure.

Council members agreed that freedom of navigation in the Red Sea must be maintained to prevent disruption to global supply chains.

Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.

The fighting has reportedly left more than 150,000 people dead and triggered one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, with more than 22 million people in need of some form of aid, according to the UN.

articles.title: Acquitted in Nithari case, Surinder Koli had two IDs — one in his own name and another as ‘Sada Ram’
articles.summary: DEHRADUN: After spending nearly 19 years in prison and escaping gallows by a few hours, Surinder Koli, 53, who was once the prime accused in the infam.
articles.body: DEHRADUN: After spending nearly 19 years in prison and escaping gallows by a few hours, Surinder Koli, 53, who was once the prime accused in the infamous Nithari case, was found hanging inside his tea kiosk in Haridwar on Friday, barely five days after starting the business. Branded the "Nithari cannibal" in a case of gruesome killings of women and children that shocked the nation, Koli was acquitted by the Supreme Court last Nov, and was now living as a "free man".Police said to hide his past, Koli was probably using a "different name" in Haridwar since most of the locals knew him as "Sada Ram". After his death, police recovered his Aadhaar card which revealed his real name.On Friday morning, customers who frequented his kiosk found it shut. "They peeped inside and found him hanging from a noose. Prima facie, it seems to be a case of suicide," said circle officer, Haridwar Shishupal Singh Negi. A panel of doctors will carry out the postmortem.Koli had two IDs, one in his own name, the other as Sada RamNo suicide note was found either on him or inside the kiosk, he said.For two decades, Koli, a Dalit from Mangaru Khal village in Uttarakhand's Almora district, who worked as a domestic help at the house of Noida-based businessman Moninder Singh Pandher, was a branded man. He was accused of being a "cannibal" who would allegedly lure children to Pandher's house, murder them, and "eat their flesh". On Dec 29, 2006, Koli and Pandher were arrested.But after a long legal battle lasting two decades and 13 death sentences later, SC, on Nov 11, passed an acquittal order in the last of the 13th cases against Koli. Two days later, he walked out a free man from Greater Noida's Luksar Jail.A few months ago, he landed in Haridwar where he had recently taken up a kiosk on a monthly rent of Rs 6,000 using his voter ID card as a validating document since it bore the name 'Sada Ram'. Prior to that, Koli was working as a security guard in Sidcul area of the town.He had worked for around 10 days as a guard but he left that job after the employers asked for his Aadhaar card. Cops have now found both the voter ID and his Aadhaar -which bore the name 'Surinder Koli' along with his Noida address. Police and the locals came to know his real identity from his Aadhaar.Almora-based social activist Narayan Singh Rawat, who had helped his family during the trials, said he suspects Koli's death to be "murder". Rawat, who hails from Almora's Salt area, had helped the family monetarily and facilitated Koli's meeting with his mother in prison."I was in regular touch with him and had recently lent him Rs 25,000 to start a tea kiosk, which he had taken on rent from a local resident linked to a political outfit. Over the phone (in the past 2-3 days), he complained of harassment. They're asking for more money, he told me... He sounded disturbed and couldn't figure out a solution," Rawat told TOI.Koli is survived by his wife, daughter and a teenaged son. His wife had started living at a relative's place in Haryana, along with their children, when he was arrested in the case in 2006. Later his wife got married again. His daughter, who was in her 20s at the time of his release from jail last year, also got married a few years ago. His mother had passed away in 2022. Among the siblings, his elder brother lives in Delhi, while his younger brother lives in Almora with his family.The younger brother told TOI, "I was in regular touch with my brother over the phone. But he never shared anything that was bothering him. We're unaware of the reason behind his suicide, as claimed by police."Stay updated with the latest Dehradun news. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: 'Can't afford petrol': Pakistan PTI lawmakers ride donkey carts to assembly in protest
articles.summary: Pakistan News: Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) workers and provincial lawmakers staged a protest in the Sindh province against soaring fuel prices. They arrived at th.
articles.body: Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) workers and provincial lawmakers staged a protest in the Sindh province against soaring fuel prices. They arrived at the provincial assembly by riding donkey carts, saying petrol had become too expensive for them to travel in their vehicles.According to Dawn news, the protest was held after petrol prices rose to Rs 390.79 per litre and high-speed diesel (HSD) to Rs 424.92 per litre following the latest adjustment on Thursday. PTI MPA Sajjad Ali and other lawmakers rode donkey carts from areas near the assembly to its main gate, carrying placards and raising slogans against the federal government.“The ministers and (treasury) MPAs should also reach the assembly the same way on donkey carts,” Ali was seen saying in a video while holding a placard describing the fuel price hike as a “petrol bomb dropped on the people”.Ali said the protest was intended to highlight the difficulties faced by ordinary people because of rising fuel costs.“Petrol has become so expensive that we cannot even come to the assembly in our vehicles,” he said, adding that people were bearing the brunt of the government’s policies.The latest increase comes amid renewed hostilities in the Middle East, which have disrupted major oil supply routes and pushed fuel prices higher over the past two months.The current petrol and diesel prices include government taxes and duties of Rs114 per litre on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel. The government now adjusts fuel prices daily.The Pakistan bar council also criticised the repeated fuel price increases. A joint meeting of its Executive Committee and Rules Committee on Thursday called the hikes unprecedented and urged the government to take steps to control prices and provide relief to citizens.The government has meanwhile introduced a relief scheme targeting users of motorcycles, rickshaws, Qingqis and other two- and three-wheelers, as well as small cars with engines up to 800cc.Under the scheme, motorcycle, rickshaw and other eligible two- and three-wheeler users can receive relief on 20 litres of petrol a month. Owners of cars with engines up to 800cc are eligible for a Rs 100-per-litre relief on 30 litres of petrol each month.However, the scheme faced problems on its first day of nationwide rollout on Thursday, with several petrol pumps refusing to accept the digital app introduced for the subsidy. The pumps said they lacked the required system to sell petrol at Rs100 per litre less.The federal government also brought back austerity measures on Thursday. articles.title: In 2003, a Montana family bought 57 acres along the Stillwater River; after cameras documented bears, wolves and mountain lions, they have permanently protected the property from development
articles.summary: US News: A Montana family has permanently protected 57 acres of riverfront land along the Stillwater River after years of documenting the wildlife that moves t.
articles.body: A Montana family has permanently protected 57 acres of riverfront land along the Stillwater River after years of documenting the wildlife that moves through the property. The conservation effort was reported by the Flathead Beacon and Whitefish Pilot, while the Flathead Land Trust confirmed details of the newly established conservation easement. Sean and Melodye Rooney purchased the land with Sean’s parents in 2003 and eventually became its sole owners. Located west of Whitefish, the property stretches along nearly a mile of the Stillwater River and is now protected under a conservation easement held by Flathead Land Trust. The agreement permanently prevents subdivision and development while allowing the Rooneys to continue living on and using the property. More than 20 acres remain in hay production, while the rest includes riparian forest, shrubland and wetlands.A wildlife corridor captured on cameraThe property’s conservation value became increasingly clear through the family’s long-term wildlife monitoring. Camera traps placed around the land have recorded an impressive range of species, including grizzly and black bears, mountain lions, gray wolves, moose, river otters and bald eagles. The land is also an official study site for Snapshot USA, a nationwide camera-trapping project that tracks changes in mammal populations across the United States.The project is coordinated nationally by the Smithsonian’s National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute and its partners. Brigit Rooney, Sean and Melodye’s daughter, serves as Snapshot USA’s survey coordinator. The programme uses standardized camera-trap surveys to study the distribution and long-term trends of mammals in relation to land use, habitat and climate.The Rooneys’ property therefore serves a purpose beyond private conservation, contributing observations to a wider scientific effort. Brigit Rooney is also a co-author of the 2026 Snapshot USA research covering the survey’s sixth year of coordinated national camera-trap data.Nearly a mile of riverfront remains protectedThe conservation easement also safeguards habitat along the Stillwater River, where wetlands and riverfront vegetation play an important role in maintaining the surrounding ecosystem.The property provides habitat for aquatic species including bull trout and westslope cutthroat trout, according to Flathead Land Trust. Its location also connects with two existing conservation easements and nearby U.S. Forest Service and Stillwater State Forest lands, creating a larger network of protected open space. The family has undertaken habitat work as well. In 2025, the Rooneys began a project aimed at restoring a ponded area and associated wetland habitat on the property.From family land to long-term conservationThe Rooneys’ connection to the Flathead Valley predates their ownership of the Stillwater property. Sean’s grandfather homesteaded near Cut Bank before working for the Great Northern Railway in Whitefish, while his father later settled in the Flathead Valley and taught English and geology at Flathead Valley Community College.The new easement means the 57-acre tract will remain undeveloped even as surrounding areas change. It preserves a combination of wildlife habitat, wetlands, river frontage and working agricultural land, while keeping the property connected to other protected areas along the Stillwater River corridor.For a landscape where wildlife monitoring has revealed bears, wolves and mountain lions using the same trails as people, providing crucial evidence of their continued presence and shared use of this landscape, the conservation agreement turns years of observation into a permanent commitment to keeping the habitat intact.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Could Northern Ireland produce WWE's next big star?
articles.summary: With a new generation of talent setting their sights on some of wrestling's biggest stages, could Northern Ireland produce its next big star?
articles.body:
For many wrestling fans growing up meant watching stars like The Rock, Stone Cold Steve Austin and John Cena on television.

But for anyone who dreamed of following in their footsteps, making it into the industry could feel a world away.

Now, those involved in the sport say opportunities are growing closer to home, giving aspiring wrestlers a chance to train, perform and begin building a career.

With a new generation setting their sights on some of the sport's biggest stages, could Northern Ireland produce the next big wrestling star?

Among those hoping to make it to the top is 16-year-old Eva, who only began training in January.

A lifelong wrestling fan, she grew up watching WWE (World Wrestling Entertainment) with her family. Discovering she could train locally turned something she watched on television into a realistic ambition.

"The reason I joined is because it's so local, it was a great opportunity because I always wanted to do something like this," she said.

Eva hopes to study performing arts after leaving school, which she believes could help develop the character and performance side of her wrestling.

She also points to Irish WWE star Becky Lynch as an inspiration, saying her success gives her "hope and motivation" that where someone comes from does not have to limit them.

Despite being only months into her wrestling journey, she has already set herself the biggest possible target.

"In the future I will be a WWE champion," she said.

Eva is one of a growing number of people turning an interest in wrestling into action by stepping into the ring.

And she isn't on her own, with one coach saying the number of people interested in the sport has "grown exponentially" in recent years.

Five years ago, the number of people training in professional wrestling across Northern Ireland was believed to be in the 30s. Today it is more than 150.

For Lisburn's Amira Blair, who appeared in the ring at Wembley Stadium last month, the route into wrestling looked very different when she was growing up.

She first dreamed of becoming a wrestler at the age of 11, but pursuing it as a career from Northern Ireland seemed a very distant prospect.

"I never thought this was a goal that you could have. It seemed like something on the TV you see Americans doing," she said.

Blair is now a full-time professional wrestler, but growing it was such a "niche thing" that she did not feel able to talk about her ambition with others.

Following that dream also meant moving from Northern Ireland to London - a decision some people struggled to understand.

"They thought I was just losing the plot and why would I not go get a normal job with stability," she added.

"Why am I moving to London on a whim and pursuing something that's just so out there?"

She says the industry has also changed significantly for women, going "from having three minutes of time in matches to getting main events".

Damien Corvin believes the gap between starting out in Northern Ireland and building a career is beginning to narrow.

He is a full-time professional wrestler and head coach at the Relentless Pro Wrestling Academy in Larne.

Corvin says aspiring wrestlers no longer necessarily have to move away to turn wrestling into a career: "It's very, very possible to be a full-time pro wrestler, for this to be your full-time job while still living in Northern Ireland.

"You can travel the world as an independent pro wrestler."

Corvin has done that himself, wrestling in India, France and Switzerland, as well as across the UK and Ireland.

He says the opportunities available to those starting out in Northern Ireland have improved significantly in recent years.

"We're giving these guys a platform to try out new characters, to try out new moves, to see what works, and get them in front of an audience," he said.

"Just watching them get that little bit better every single week is amazing as a coach, but it also leads me to have high hopes for the future of what we can do in Northern Ireland wrestling."

Carrickfergus man Dylan Todd, known in the ring as DD Crooks, is among those hoping to turn wrestling into a career.

Growing up, he was more interested in drama and skateboarding than traditional sports and despite being a wrestling fan, did not realise it was something he could pursue locally.

He says being around wrestlers who have progressed in the industry makes it feel much more achievable.

"When you see those guys doing it and you're like, 'well, it wasn't long ago they were probably in my position'," he said.

Dylan believes the "immense" talent currently coming through across the island of Ireland could lead to more wrestlers making their mark in the ring.

"I'd sleep outside if it meant getting a job wrestling one day. Honestly, it's my dream job," he added.

articles.title: Lockheed Martin refines design of stealth unmanned fighter Vectis, as India readies its CATS Warrior
articles.summary: International News: As the realm of aerial combat moves towards greater automation, US firm Lockheed Martin's Skunk Works has lifted the veil further on Vectis, a stealth.
articles.body: As the realm of aerial combat moves towards greater automation, US firm Lockheed Martin's Skunk Works has lifted the veil further on Vectis, a stealthy Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) first unveiled in September last year, revealing new details ahead of the Air, Space & Cyber Conference. The standout feature is its air intake, deeply recessed into the top of the fuselage behind a downward-sloping v-shaped channel, a configuration that is far more elaborate than earlier renderings of the aircraft suggested, this approach is very different from the intake of the domestically still underdevelopment CATS Warrior.Vectis is also notable for being the first tailless CCA design to emerge from a US manufacturer, featuring a lambda wing planform, a prominent set of chine lines and a arrowhead shaped nose. At roughly 34 feet long with a 38-foot wingspan, it's comparable in size to the Navy's T-45 Goshawk trainer. According to Skunk Works, the department of the company that works on stealthy aircraft, the submerged inlet reduces frontal drag for better range, while also protecting against foreign object debris when operating from austere runways in the Pacific, a nod to the Air Force's Agile Combat Employment (ACE) concept.Construction of the first prototype is already underway, with Lockheed targeting a first flight by the end of next year, and four more prototypes planned using internal funding. The firm has highlighted the speed of development, from napkin sketch to wind tunnel validation in under two months, first digital build in six months and first part release in eight, crediting advanced digital engineering and a technique called minimal tooling determinant assembly, which has reportedly cut labour hours by up to 80%.On capability, Vectis is expected to handle both air-to-air and air-to-ground missions, with promotional visuals showing it launching AIM-120 AMRAAMs and GBU-53/B StormBreaker glide bombs from an internal weapons bay accommodating at least two munitions, alongside an electro-optical/infrared sensor turret.India is building its own answer to this technology through two parallel programmes. The Ghatak stealth drone, a flying-wing unmanned combat aerial vehicle powered by a dry variant of the indigenous Kaveri engine, is being developed by DRDO to carry precision-guided munitions deep into contested airspace, without risking a pilot.Alongside this, HAL is working on the aforementioned CATS Warrior under its Combat Air Teaming System programme, a twin-engine unmanned platform powered by the domestically developed PTAE-7, designed to fly alongside existing fighters like the Tejas Mk-1A, Su-30 MKI and Jaguar, as well as future platforms including the Tejas Mk-2 and India's fifth-generation AMCA. Together, these efforts mark a serious push toward self-reliance in advanced unmanned combat systems.With China, Russia, Turkey and France all pursuing similar flying-wing designs, Vectis stands out as arguably the closest thing to a stealthy uncrewed combat aircraft to emerge from the CCA programme so far.

articles.title: AI helps recycle old milk bottles into new plastic packaging
articles.summary: AI identifies crushed plastic milk bottles at Redcar plant, helping turn waste into new packaging.
articles.body:
Artificial intelligence is being used to help turn old milk bottles into new ones and they can be back in your fridge "within two weeks".

Recycling site Biffa Polymers in Redcar uses the technology to analyse materials moving along conveyor belts at a speed and scale that "would be difficult for people to match".

Managing director James McLeary, said AI could identify different types of plastic using optical and infra-red scanning, as well as image analysis.

But he said the plant still relied on a workforce of about 200 people who are freed up by AI to ensure products are of the right quality, rather than "spending their time doing tedious tasks".

The technology can analyse images of waste and identify a material's composition.

McLeary said that was "particularly useful" when bottles have been crushed or distorted and they were trying to select high-density polyethylene (HDPE) bottles, which can be recycled for food-grade packaging.

"A milk bottle might be easy to recognise when it is intact, but once crushed its shape can change completely.

"AI systems can be trained to recognise that the different shapes are still milk bottles," he said.

The Redcar plant - which has now processed the equivalent of more than 10 billion plastic milk bottles in almost 20 years - takes plastic which has already been sorted by type and colour and carries out the final stages of processing.

Material is shredded, washed and separated before being treated and turned into fine plastic pellets.

Those pellets can then be used to produce new packaging, including food-grade material for milk bottles.

The company said it was investigating in other robotic systems which could use AI to physically pick out those bottles.

It also uses AI for safety around the site, monitoring cameras and identifying "potential risks... for example, when someone appears to be moving into an area where a vehicle could be operating".

But McLeary said the plant remained reliant on its workforce despite the growing role of technology and that they still need people who are "prepared to do good, hard labour on the lines, sorting stuff very responsibly".

He added that the technology was allowing the recycling process to speed up.

"[A] bottle that you threw away two weeks ago may be back in somebody else's fridge, because that's how quickly the material gets recycled in the UK," McLeary said.

articles.title: Meet Kent Hups, the Colorado teacher who spotted three strange toes in North Dakota and helped uncover the first adult T. rex trackway
articles.summary: US News: Kent Hups, a Colorado high school teacher and amateur fossil hunter, was looking for an easier route out of a narrow, rocky valley in North Dakota's b.
articles.body: Kent Hups, a Colorado high school teacher and amateur fossil hunter, was looking for an easier route out of a narrow, rocky valley in North Dakota's badlands in 2025 when he noticed something unusual protruding from the ground. To Hups, who had spent about 30 years searching for ancient footprints as a hobby, the lumpy, wedge-shaped rock looked like three giant toes. He was volunteering with a fossil-digging team led by palaeontologist Tyler Lyson when he contacted him about the discovery. Lyson was sceptical and wanted more than a single unusual shape before accepting it as a dinosaur track. Further excavation revealed a sequence of four three-toed footprints stretching about 23 feet across the hillside. Researchers have identified an adult Tyrannosaurus rex as the most likely trackmaker, making it the first described trackway likely left by an adult T. rex. The approximately 66.5-million-year-old trail provides evidence of the dinosaur in motion, something that fossilised bones cannot show on their own.Lyson wanted a pattern, not just one footprintHups found the first footprint while prospecting for fossils in the Hell Creek Formation. He measured and photographed the unusual structure before contacting Lyson, a senior curator of vertebrate palaeontology at the Denver Museum of Nature & Science. At the time, scientists had identified only two adult T. rex footprints anywhere in the world, one in New Mexico and one in Montana, making the possibility of a third particularly significant.When Hups returned to the site the following day with companions, they identified another possible track. Lyson remained unconvinced and said he wanted to see a pattern. According to National Geographic's account of the discovery, Lyson marked a location where a third footprint should appear if the structures formed a genuine trackway. Excavation there revealed another footprint, followed by a fourth. The resulting sequence records two left and two right footprints. The published study titled A large tridactyl trackway from the Upper Cretaceous Hell Creek Formation of North Dakota, likely attributable to an adult Tyrannosaurus rex, describes the trackway as approximately 7 metres long, with the footprints each measuring roughly 1 metre in length. The distinction between an isolated footprint and a trackway is important. A single print can provide information about foot size and shape, but a sequence shows how an animal moved. In this case, the spacing between the prints gives researchers a stride of about 13 feet and allows them to estimate the dinosaur's walking speed.The Hell Creek Formation rarely preserves dinosaur footprintsThe discovery was made in the Hell Creek Formation of southwestern North Dakota, near Marmarth, on federal land administered by the U.S. Forest Service. The rocks formed about 66.5 million years ago in an environment that included forested floodplains, streams and swampy areas. The formation is particularly famous for dinosaur bones, including T. rex and Triceratops, but footprints are far rarer. The watery environment may help explain why. Sediment and flowing water could disturb or erase footprints before they became preserved. In this case, Lyson and his colleagues hypothesise that the three-toed depressions filled with warm, sandy water containing bacteria soon after the animal walked through. Sediments and minerals then accumulated in the hollows, eventually producing a dense mixture of calcium carbonate and sandstone around the footprints. Erosion later removed softer surrounding material and exposed the hardened structures.The resulting fossils are unusual because they are not simply shallow impressions in a layer of rock. National Geographic reported that the tracks are preserved in three-dimensional sandstone concretions, allowing the shape of the animal's foot to remain visible even after tens of millions of years. Researchers have found only one other trackway of any kind in the Hell Creek Formation, and it was not attributed to either T. rex or Triceratops.Nearby T. rex fossils helped identify the trackmakerScientists cannot normally determine a dinosaur's exact species from a footprint alone. Different animals can produce similar three-toed tracks, so researchers considered several lines of evidence when identifying the North Dakota trackmaker. The footprints are exceptionally large, roughly 3 feet long, and have a narrow three-toed shape. The surrounding area also contains abundant T. rex fossils. The researchers therefore identified T. rex as the most likely trackmaker rather than claiming that the footprints alone prove the species. The scientific description says the identification is supported by the tracks' size and morphology together with the abundance of T. rex fossils in the surrounding area.Other fossils found nearby add context. Lyson's team previously recovered a juvenile T. rex nicknamed Teen Rex, located a little more than 10 miles from the trackway. The team also excavated a largely intact Triceratops specimen nicknamed Triceratops Dreams less than half a mile away. A fragment of a tyrannosaur tooth was found on the lower jaw of that Triceratops, although researchers could not determine which tyrannosaur species the tooth came from.The tracks could reveal how T. rex movedThe four footprints provide a rare behavioural record. The trackway contains two left and two right prints, with an estimated stride of about 13 feet. Researchers estimate that the animal was moving at roughly 3.5 to 4.5 miles per hour, comparable to a brisk human walking pace. Because the tracks are heavily weathered, the speed estimate remains approximate. High-resolution 3D surface scanning has preserved detailed digital models of the entire trackway, allowing researchers to examine the footprints remotely and create physical reproductions. Three of the fossilised tracks are scheduled to be recovered by helicopter and transported to the Denver Museum of Nature & Science for preparation and further research. Scientists hope the specimens could provide additional information about T. rex foot anatomy, biomechanics and potentially even skin impressions. For Hups, the discovery began with a strange shape in a landscape where he had spent years searching for fossils. What emerged from the rock was not a T. rex skeleton, but a much rarer record of the animal actually walking across the ancient landscape. As Hups put it, a track shows the size of the living foot itself, including the dimensions that bones alone cannot fully convey.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 2014, Leonardo DiCaprio's foundation donated $1 million, helping save African elephants who were being killed for their ivory tusks at a rate of 100 per day
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Illegal hunting and the ivory trade have reduced the populations of elephants in Africa drastically over the past century. Millions of these mammals o.
articles.body: Illegal hunting and the ivory trade have reduced the populations of elephants in Africa drastically over the past century. Millions of these mammals once roamed the iconic jungles, but their long ivory tusks made them targets of big game hunters and poachers who have decimated their numbers by roughly 95% over the past 100 years. The ivory trade drives a brutal campaign of international poaching that killed 22,000 elephants in 2012 alone, despite a global ban on the sale of ivory.According to the World Wildlife Fund for Nature (WWF), there are an estimated 415,000 African elephants, but other organisations put their numbers even lower, claiming that those "may ultimately prove to be optimistic."In order to save the elephants, a joint initiative was launched by Save the Elephants and the Wildlife Conservation Network, titled the Elephant Crisis Fund. Started in 2013, it had an initial target of raising $5 million over three years to provide funding for global projects to stop poaching, trafficking and the demand for ivory.In 2014, at a gala in Malibu held in support of the fund, they made major progress toward the goal. Hollywood legend Leonardo DiCaprio ended up giving the initiative not only his star power, but also a $1 million grant from his foundation, the Leonardo DiCaprio Foundation. “Elephant poaching is a brutal crisis, with more than 30,000 elephants killed last year alone. The decimation of these animals is something we have the power to stop, and the Elephant Crisis Fund is a crucial part of the solution,” said the Hollywood actor in a statement. In total, the Elephant Crisis Fund raised $2 million during the 2014 Malibu gala.Douglas-Hamilton, a researcher who has spent more than 50 years studying elephants in the wild, is the founder of Save the Elephants. “The only future for elephants is for governments, organisations, and individuals to join together in their support,” said Douglas-Hamilton back in 2014. “What we have seen in Los Angeles has given us greater hope than ever, as a generous donation by the Leonardo DiCaprio Foundation was matched by this astonishing community.”The event was attended by a number of Hollywood stars including director Rupert Wyatt, singer Barbra Streisand, actor Jonah Hill, Glee star Dianna Agron, actor Dermot Mulroney, Snow White And The Huntsman actress Liberty Ross, Interscope Records co-founder Jimmy Iovine, and Mad Men actress Elisabeth Moss.Then in 2016, Netflix released a documentary, 'The Ivory Game', produced by DiCaprio, that Indiewire described as 'a real-life ecological thriller' about the illegal ivory trade. “If James Bond turned his attention to animal rights issues, he might find himself in the middle of this hidden war,” the publication said.That same year, the United States took action to stop illegal poaching and protect endangered elephants by imposing a near-total ban on the commercial trade of African elephant ivory in order to reduce global demand. Many countries followed suit, including Hong Kong, which was the primary transit and processing hub, and China, which overtook Japan as the world’s largest importer of ivory in the 2000s.Over the past ten years, the Environmental Investigation Agency (EIA), says that elephant poaching and ivory trafficking have gone down overall. However, other groups still state numbers in excess of 30,000 as there is no hard reliable data. “The only future for elephants is for governments, organisations, and individuals to join together in their support,” said Iain Douglas-Hamilton, founder of Save The Elephants.Over the years, DiCaprio has been heavily invested in animal conservation. In 2013, he hosted an art auction raising $38.8M for global conservation initiatives. His foundation has given $3 million for Oceana’s ocean conservation programs and $3 million for WWF’s tiger program in Nepal.Recently, he and the Bezos Earth Fund launched the Phoenix Species Project, an initiative dedicated to recovering endangered species. The $200M fund will provide support to recover 100 species facing imminent extinction spanning mammals, amphibians, reptiles, birds, fish, invertebrates and plants from 30 countries in habitats ranging from oceans to volcanic plains.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: The man considered the world's last royal coachmaker died at 76 before finishing a 3-tonne carriage for King Charles III; his team says it is now 98% complete
articles.summary: Rest of World News: For more than half a century, Jim Frecklington turned wood, metal, leather and gold into something increasingly rare: magnificent horse-drawn carriage.
articles.body: For more than half a century, Jim Frecklington turned wood, metal, leather and gold into something increasingly rare: magnificent horse-drawn carriages built by hand. His workshop on Sydney's northern beaches became the unlikely birthplace of vehicles destined for royal ceremonies, but his final project was also his most personal. Frecklington died at 76, leaving behind a three-tonne carriage for King Charles III that is now nearly complete, states an online report by ABC Information and Services. Scroll down to read the details.A final gift to the crownFrecklington died in an aged care facility in Manly after a lengthy battle with cancer. Despite receiving a terminal diagnosis while the Commonwealth Royal Coach was still under construction, he continued working toward completing the decade-long project, adds the report. The carriage is now about 98 percent finished, according to members of his team, who are completing the final details, the report said. The enormous coach was financed in part by remortgaging Frecklington's home and was designed as a tribute to more than 1,000 years of British monarchy and the Commonwealth.If we go by the online reports, its details reflect the extraordinary level of craftsmanship that went into the project. Hand-applied gold leaf covers much of the coach, while timber from Westminster Abbey forms part of its construction. Despite its traditional appearance, the carriage incorporates modern comforts, including electric windows and air conditioning.From a pony cart to royal carriagesFrecklington's fascination with coachmaking began when he was just eight years old. Growing up in Parkes, New South Wales, he struggled to ride his Shetland pony and found another solution which was of building a cart for the animal to pull. That childhood experiment eventually led him around the world. After graduating from The Scots College in Sydney in 1968, Frecklington spent time in the Arctic operating heavy equipment used in the construction of airstrips. He moved to England four years later and worked at Windsor Castle, caring for the Duke of Edinburgh's four-in-hand horses, states ABC report. He later joined the Royal Mews in London, where he worked with Queen Elizabeth II's ceremonial horses.A legacy built on wheelsFrecklington's connection to the British royal family continued after he returned to Australia. In 1977, he was invited to manage Queen Elizabeth II's Silver Jubilee Exhibition during its Australian tour and created a replica of Edward VII's 1902 State Landau. His work soon reached an even grander scale. He built the Australian State Coach as Australia's Bicentennial gift to Queen Elizabeth II in 1988 and later created the Diamond Jubilee State Coach for her 80th birthday in 2006. According to the report, the Diamond Jubilee coach eventually played a role in King Charles III's coronation because the Commonwealth Royal Coach was not yet ready.A craft that may never be repeatedFrecklington leaves behind three carriages associated with the British royal family and a reputation built on craftsmanship rather than mass production. His approach was famously hands-on, relying heavily on experience and an ability to visualize complex designs without conventional plans. Now, his final carriage is being completed by the craftsmen who worked alongside him. When finished, the Commonwealth Royal Coach will stand as more than a ceremonial vehicle. It will be the final chapter of a remarkable career and a lasting example of a traditional craft that Frecklington spent his life keeping alive.Images Courtesy: ABC Information and ServicesCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Hummingbird hawk moths and ivy bees: The insects growing in number as temperatures rise
articles.summary: Hummingbird hawk moths - often mistaken for small birds - are being spotted in the West Midlands.
articles.body:
As parts of the West Midlands baked in warmer temperatures this summer, species once considered unusual in the region, such as hummingbird hawk moths, ivy bees and the wasp spider have been spotted in growing numbers.

The hummingbird hawk moth, known for its furry grey body, orange hindwings and long proboscis, migrates to the UK from southern Europe and north Africa in the summer months.

James Benwell, from the Birmingham and Black Country Wildlife Trust, said 2026 was a "record year" for sightings of the species, which was often mistaken for a small bird.

The moth, which can be seen hovering over flowers, has wings that beat about 80 times per second , according to Benwell.

"They've had a really good year this year," he said. "Normally they would come in small numbers. We'd normally hear of a few maybe. But this year, we've seen loads of records of them.

"They're absolutely amazing but I somehow haven't seen one this year, so I'm jealous of anybody else that has."

Ivy bees, which feed mainly on the nectar of ivy flowers, had also become more prevalent in the Midlands, Benwell said, adding they were easy to find on buildings.

The bees, first recorded in the UK in 2001, are slowly spreading north, after first being recorded in the region in Stourbridge in 2015.

"There's nothing that distinguishes them from other bees really, they're not that kind of attention-grabbing species, but, you know, were you to look for them, go to ivy and you'll see them," Benwell said.

Other insects that had seen an increase in their numbers locally included the clouded yellow butterfly, a European migratory species known to have "peak" years during unusually hot summers.

"Most individuals are unable to survive the British winter, but if temperatures continue to rise as a result of climate change, we may well see them becoming permanent residents," Benwell said.

"There's numerous species that we could point out that weren't here 20 years ago... and now they're quite abundant."

Others once more commonly associated with southern England have also spread further north.

The trust said the hornet hoverfly, with yellow markings that mimic a hornet to protect against predators, although it cannot sting, had become really common after it was first recorded in Birmingham and the Black Country in 2004.

Another species, the cricket bat spider, which gets its name from its cricket bat-like markings, has also become more common in grassland since it was first spotted in the region in 2019.

The sightings come as one of the UK's largest spider species, the wasp spider, was spotted in the Midlands as warmer temperatures pushed it more than 100 miles away from its usual habitat.

The spider has recently been recorded in Worcestershire, alongside sightings in Herefordshire and Warwickshire, said the Worcestershire Wildlife Trust.

Rosemary Winnall, from the Wyre Forest Study Group, which maps the wildlife and ecology of the forest in Worcestershire, said the arrival of the wasp spider was to be celebrated.

She said the group was always on the lookout for new arrivals and had already recorded the willow emerald damselfly, the southern oak bush cricket and the purple emperor butterfly, as more species travelled north.

"The impressive western conifer seed bug is here as is the box bug," she added.

Hot weather had also benefited butterflies that loved sunshine, such as the holly blue and the pearl-bordered fritillary, which the Butterfly Conservation charity said was once "very widespread" but had rapidly declined in recent decades.

However, despite an increase in some species appearing in the region, there were others whose numbers were dwindling.

"The once-common small tortoiseshell butterfly is now rarely seen for example, and there are far fewer records of the two-spot ladybird," Winnall explained.

"We are encouraging folk to record the common species of today as they may be the rarities of the future."
